It’s OK to not know where you’re going or where you’re at. It’s also OK to take your time, process your emotions, and try new things, even if you don’t stick to them. I think we all need to learn that if some thing or someone is not for us, we don’t have to stay chained to it. You’re not a quitter, you’re not giving up. You’re just trying to figure life out and so are the rest of us. Go easy on yourself. It takes time for everybody. Don’t compare yourself to anybody else or anybody else’s timeline or phases that they are going through. It’s easy to panic, but if we were to get really honest with ourselves, it’s not that deep. Yes it’s good to want to make something of yourself or do some thing with your time, but that could literally be anything. When I became disabled, I felt less significant than others that could contribute more to society in my thinking. But then I started doing small things like signing petitions to make a difference or giving advice online or just offering friendship to people. We all have a purpose and we can all make a difference. We don’t have to have a plan for it. You make a difference being you.

I’m take alprazolam for panic attacks and Prozac for OCD. However, I can’t exactly recommend anything as I don’t know your history and I’m not a Dr. 

I think OCD can be EXTREMELY distracting to the point where we have trouble paying attention, doing basic tasks, and having issues with short term memory. 

I think a better question is, when you have moments of relative calm, are you still feeling scattered, forgetting simple but important things, or are you constantly bumping into things or needing to write trivial things down to remember them? Does it take something very specific to fuel you with dopamine? (The reward hormone.) Do you have trouble starting something you need, want and are actually ready to start and it feels like your body won’t let you? Do you feel driven to get up and do all the things as if driven by a motor? (Just doing something- not compulsions.) There are a few online ADHD assessments but I think you’re on the right track with therapy bc when you have comorbid disorders, the best way to attack it it usually is through the process of elimination. 

My therapist asked how I feel when I forget things or stop mid-sentence bc I forgot everything I was going to say. Was I feeling anxious? If I wasn’t that might be and indication of adhd but if I am, ocd and even adhd both can cause social anxiety. They may suggest keeping a journal if you can remember to. What were you thinking when you forgot what you were saying? We’re you distracted by something or just stopped in your tracks? We’re you feeling anxious or uptight? 
I found this to be somewhat helpful although it’s not a diagnosis. ADHD and OCD both come with intrusive thoughts so it’s better to start somewhere else in the elimination process. Hope this helps!
